review.title: Overview
review.body:
STRATEGIC BUSINESS REVIEW

Persepolis Foods Group

2025 performance and 2026 planning outlook | A fictional global nutrition and consumer goods business

INDEPENDENT TEACHING CASE — ALL COMPANY NAMES, BRANDS, FIGURES, TARGETS AND EVENTS ARE FICTIONAL.

Who we are

Persepolis Foods Group is a fictional multinational producer of food, beverages, nutrition products and pet care solutions. Headquartered in the fictional city of Shiraz, Iran, the group operates through manufacturing, research, retail partnerships and digital channels in more than 70 markets. Its portfolio balances established everyday brands with premium and health-oriented products.

Portfolio at a glance

Four operating divisions provide complementary revenue streams. The business combines consumer packaged goods scale with specialised nutrition expertise and a growing direct-to-consumer presence.

Operating footprint

The group operates across 28 markets, with a regional mix of 44% Europe, 31% Asia-Pacific and 25% Americas by sales. The portfolio spans everyday staples, premium nutrition and specialised pet products. Retail consolidation, private-label competition and commodity price volatility create distinct pressures across these regions. All market shares and operating data are fictional.

Persepolis has 42 production facilities, approximately 38,000 employees and a distribution network serving supermarkets, convenience retailers, foodservice customers and online marketplaces. Its operating model combines centralised research and brand governance with local category and market teams.

The management challenge

After several years of inflation and changes in consumer purchasing behaviour, Persepolis must rebuild volume growth without sacrificing margins. Leadership has identified digital capability, portfolio focus, supply chain resilience and customer trust as critical enablers of future performance.

review.title: 01 / STRATEGIC IDENTITY
review.body:
01 / STRATEGIC IDENTITY

Purpose, vision and values

The strategic direction against which every Balanced Scorecard objective should be tested.

Our purpose

To make everyday nourishment more accessible, enjoyable and responsible for people, families and their pets.

Our vision

To become the most trusted, innovative and sustainably profitable nutrition and food group in our chosen markets by 2030.

Our mission

We create affordable and premium food and nutrition solutions through consumer insight, responsible sourcing, product innovation and operational excellence.

Core values

Strategic intent

The group seeks a balance between sustainable growth, strong customer relationships, resilient processes and employee capability. The board has instructed management to translate this intent into a strategy map with measurable outcomes and clear initiatives.

review.title: 02 / STRATEGY
review.body:
02 / STRATEGY

Six strategic pillars

A coherent programme linking market outcomes to the capabilities required to deliver them.

Strategic interdependence

Digital and analytical capabilities can improve forecasting and production efficiency. Faster innovation and better distribution can improve customer experience and brand preference. These customer outcomes are expected to support revenue growth, profitability and cash generation. These links are management hypotheses for evaluation, not guaranteed causal effects.

Priority risks

Risk interdependencies: a packaging redesign may reduce material use but increase unit costs; agricultural sourcing improvements may improve traceability while exposing the group to supplier concentration; rapid innovation can create execution and food-safety risks. Management therefore evaluates strategic decisions against margin, consumer value, operational continuity and environmental impact together.

Management monitors raw-material inflation, exchange-rate movements, retail price pressure, food safety, supply disruption, cyber security, climate exposure and employee capability gaps. Each pillar must therefore be supported by measurable indicators and initiatives rather than broad aspirations.

2026 planning assumptions

The 2026 plan assumes a modest recovery in consumer demand, selective pricing, continued marketing investment and phased operational savings. Forecast outcomes remain uncertain and depend on market conditions.

Revenue growth is forecast at 4.0% for 2026, while operating margin is expected to rise from 14.9% to 15.8%. Management attributes the planned improvement to portfolio prioritisation, operational simplification and more efficient commercial spending.

review.title: 05 / EXECUTION
review.body:
05 / EXECUTION

2026 outlook, sustainability and resilience

An integrated outlook covering responsible growth, environmental stewardship and operational resilience.

Management programmes

The 2026–2028 transformation programme combines selective brand investment, product renovation, omnichannel availability, automated planning and procurement simplification. Alongside these commercial programmes, Persepolis plans to trial low-carbon heat at selected sites, redesign flexible packaging, establish supplier due-diligence protocols and introduce water-risk assessments. The board will monitor investment returns, affordability, food safety and sustainability trade-offs; some initiatives may increase near-term costs before delivering longer-term savings.

Sustainability commitments and governance

Governance model: a board-level sustainability and risk committee reviews quarterly progress; procurement owns supplier assessment, operations owns site energy and water, packaging teams own design standards, and internal audit tests data quality. The company has not sought external assurance for the fictional indicators in this case.

Persepolis has established a fictional sustainability roadmap for 2026–2030. Its priorities are reducing operational emissions, improving water efficiency at high-risk facilities, increasing recyclable or reusable packaging and strengthening supplier traceability. The group aims to balance commercial expansion with resource stewardship and product safety. All figures and commitments in this case are illustrative.

Environmental and social performance indicators

Management estimates that 2025 Scope 1 and 2 emissions were 410,000 tonnes CO₂e, compared with a 2022 baseline of 500,000 tonnes. Its illustrative 2030 ambition is a 45% reduction against that baseline. In 2025, 68% of consumer packaging by weight was designed for recycling; the 2030 aspiration is 95%. Water intensity at priority sites was 3.4 m³ per tonne of finished product, with a 2028 ambition of 2.8 m³. The proportion of priority agricultural inputs traceable to an assessed supplier was 74%, with a 2028 ambition of 95%. These indicators are fictional and are not externally assured.

Source and intellectual-property note

This independently written fictional case is not affiliated with or endorsed by any real company.

review.title: 06 / Reconciliation & calculation supplement
review.body: The supplied instructor key uses illustrative ROA inputs of £240m net profit and £3,000m average assets. These are a separate teaching scenario, not the review’s 2025 results (£1,745m profit, £24,000m closing assets). The review does not supply 2024 opening assets, so 2025 ROA cannot be established using average assets. Supplementary opening/closing balances of £2,800m/£3,200m are explicitly assumed for the £240m ROA exercise. Market share £600m/£5,000m and certification 300/600 are instructor-key illustrations. The review states both more than 70 markets and 28 markets; scope requires instructor reconciliation. FCF convention for this game: operating cash flow less capital expenditure; detailed cash flows are not provided. Weighted distribution uses category-sales weights. Vision statements and causal map are editorial teaching interpretations of the supplied review, pending instructor review.
